content: There is a growing global burden of injuries, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). To address this issue, trauma care models originally developed in high-income countries are being implemented in LMICs. One such strategy involves training ambulance crews in advanced life support (ALS) to improve outcomes for trauma patients. However, the effectiveness of this intervention remains controversial, and the available evidence has not been rigorously evaluated. The objective of this study was to determine whether ALS-trained ambulance crews are more effective than crews without ALS training in reducing mortality and morbidity among trauma patients. A comprehensive search for relevant studies was conducted on May 16, 2014, using multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others. Reference lists were also screened for additional studies. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed randomized controlled trials, controlled trials, and non-randomized studies, such as before-and-after studies and interrupted time series studies. These studies needed to compare the outcomes of trauma patients treated by ALS-trained ambulance crews versus those treated by crews without ALS training. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion and extracted relevant data. The review identified three studies that met the inclusion criteria: one controlled before-and-after trial, one uncontrolled before-and-after study, and one randomized controlled trial. None of these studies provided evidence to support the effectiveness of ALS training for pre-hospital personnel. In the uncontrolled before-and-after study, a pre-specified subgroup analysis revealed an increase in mortality among patients with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of less than nine who were treated by ALS-trained crews. Furthermore, when the pre-hospital trauma score was included in a logistic regression analysis, mortality rates were found to be significantly higher in patients receiving care from ALS-trained crews. Based on the current evidence, there is no indication that advanced life support training for ambulance crews improves patient outcomes. In fact, some findings suggest that it may be associated with worse outcomes in certain subgroups of trauma patients.
